The bastard grunt, Pomadasys incisus, is a coastal demersal species for which key life-history parameters have been estimated from congeneric data and allometric relationships. Field-based surveys and morphometric analyses indicate that the ultimate total length attainable by this species is 53.5 cm [Li = 53.5 cm], representing the maximum recorded size for an adult individual. This value, derived from observed specimens, positions P. incisus among the larger members of its genus found in the eastern Atlantic. Complementing this length estimate, the wet weight at puberty has been calculated based on the length-weight relationship established for the species. Individuals reaching the pubertal length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm], a figure drawn from data on the congener Pomadasys maculatus, attain a corresponding somatic mass of approximately 63 grams [Wwp = approximately 63 grams] at that developmental milestone. The transition to reproductive maturity thus involves a considerable increase from the larval stage to a size capable of supporting gametogenesis. These morphometric benchmarks are fundamental for understanding the species' reproductive ecology and for constructing population models that assess its response to fishing pressure.

Reproductive output in Pomadasys incisus has been characterized using fecundity estimates from the closely related species Pomadasys jubelini. Under stable thermal conditions typical of its coastal habitat (23.1 °C [T = 23.1 °C]), a mature female of 25 cm total length is estimated to produce a single clutch of approximately 146,963 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 146,963 eggs per spawning event]. Given that this species is thought to spawn only once per season, the annual reproductive output reaches approximately 403 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 403 eggs per day]. The combination of a large clutch size and a single spawning event yields a substantial daily reproductive output that supports the species' potential for population replenishment in its coastal habitat. Such high daily fecundity is typical of tropical batch spawners, where it compensates for high egg and larval mortality rates in the plankton.

At 23.1 °C [T = 23.1 °C], the early life stages of this species are characterized by a minimal initial size that belies its rapid growth potential. The wet weight at birth, based on the egg diameter of 0.85 mm typical of similar-sized lutjanids, is estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], representing the mass of the newly fertilized, yolk-laden egg. This tiny initial mass (0.00032 grams) [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] underscores the extreme vulnerability of the pelagic egg stage to predation and advection. The total incubation and yolk-sac absorption period is brief; the age at hatching and subsequent mouth opening is estimated at approximately seven days [ab = approximately seven days] at a temperature of 23.1 °C [T = 23.1 °C]. This rapid transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic larval stage is critical, as the timing of first exogenous feeding must coincide with the availability of suitable planktonic prey. The combination of a minute birth mass and a short embryonic period is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early feeding onset and rapid larval development.

Adult body size in Pomadasys incisus ultimately plateaus at a maximum wet weight of 1908 grams [Wwi = 1908 grams], a value derived from the allometric length-weight relationship (coefficient 0.01349) applied to the ultimate total length. This asymptotic mass represents the heaviest individuals recorded in the population, typically attained after several years of sustained growth. The substantial increase from the pubertal mass of 63 grams [Wwp = 63 grams] to this ultimate mass reflects a prolonged period of post-maturational growth, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts that experience indeterminate growth. The ultimate body mass is a key determinant of maximal fecundity and competitive ability in the spawning aggregation, as larger females can accommodate more ovarian tissue and produce larger clutches over successive spawning events. Consequently, protecting older, larger individuals is essential for maintaining the reproductive potential of the stock.

Longevity in Pomadasys incisus has been estimated from captive observations and age-validation studies on related species. Under a controlled thermal regime maintained at 23.1 °C [T = 23.1 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately seven years [am = approximately seven years]. This value positions the bastard grunt as a moderate-lived species within the Haemulidae family, comparable to other coastal grunts that experience moderate natural mortality. The lifespan is likely influenced by both temperature and food availability in the wild; individuals in cooler, more productive waters may exhibit slightly reduced metabolic rates and consequently extended longevity. The completion of this lifespan is generally marked by natural mortality associated with senescence and the progressive deterioration of physiological systems rather than by a catastrophic spawning event. Understanding the species' maximum age is critical for calculating its turnover rate and for setting appropriate harvest limits in artisanal fisheries where it is a common catch component.
